title: Janelle Shane: The Baltimore Orioles Effect: Hey! Stop poisoning my image prompt!
speaker: Janelle Shane
talk_title: The Baltimore Orioles Effect: Hey! Stop poisoning my image prompt!
description:
When the Baltimore Orioles are both a baseball team and a species of bird, online-trained image generating algorithms like DALL-E tend to get confused. Through funny images of a baseball team buying huge bags of oranges at the grocery store, or birds flying to Florida in an airplane, I explore what happens when AI has seen your phrase in another sense online.

Lead-in music generated by Sonat Uzun

their bird form it looks like. And they also can make it so that giraffes can attend the
birthday party as well. I don't know why they are all turning away from the camera in the
last one. They can imagine salmon at a birthday party. The Baltimore Orioles effect is when
the thing you trying to generate appears incompletely different ways on the internet and the result
can be funny from highly to distressing. It affects text generators, image generators,
pretty much anything built on internet-scraped data because somewhere elsewhere on the internet
there may be a fictional version of you or your name or ethnicity especially if you are
marginalized in some way. There could be a version of you on the internet in someplace
where people are using your name, using your thing, where everyone thinks you are mean,
bad or fond of oranges and then an internet trained AI may have learned that version of
you too and that will come out in stuff built on that AI. This is a classic case of a researcher
robin Spear who was using internet data to build a system that could analyze, look at
text reviews and analyze how people were rating various things. She found this system thought
people hated the Mexican restaurants even though the reviews were quite positive. She
analyzed the situation and found that this particular system trained on how people used
text on the internet thought that the word Mexican was a bad thing based on how certain
parts of the internet were using the word. The lesson to take from the Baltimore Orioles
effect is that it effects a lot of people, it effects a lot of things and comes up in
several ways. If you are thinking of -- affects -- building something or somebody wants you
to build something that relies on internet trained AI in some form you need to think
really carefully about it because there is a risk you will build something that will
not work well for some people, not going to be fun for some people, or that ends up doing
something distressing or really embarrassing. This effect can be really sneaky when it shows
up and it be hard to auto filter as well. We have this Snickers logo and we have sneakers
showing up. That would be really hard to see this sort of thing creeping in ahead of time.
This goes to show when people talk then about the training data for image generators as
a lot of people have been talking about this lately quite often the focus is on the artist
whose work is included without their permission. But we should also be remembering about the
training data, the other training data. That's not necessarily composed of art but it is
still having an effect on whatever we are trying to generate. Skewing it in ways that
might be hard to detect or hard to prevent. Skewing in ways we really might not want.
With all of this, I would like you to keep in mind that the Baltimore Orioles Effect
is a thing you never quite know when it is going to strike. Thank you very much.
